Enlarge this image Mike Morgan/NPR Mike Morgan/NPR Andrea Hsu Labor and Workplace Correspondent Andrea Hsu is NPR's labor and workplace correspondent. Hsu first joined NPR in 2002 and spent nearly two decades as a producer for All Things Considered . Through interviews and in-depth series, she's covered topics ranging from America's opioid epidemic to emerging research at the intersection of music and the brain . She led the award-winning NPR team that happened to be in Sichuan Province, China, when a massive earthquake struck in 2008. In the coronavirus pandemic, she reported a series of stories on the pandemic's uneven toll on women , capturing the angst that women and especially mothers were experiencing across the country, alone. Hsu came to NPR via National Geographic, the BBC, and the long-shuttered Jumping Cow Coffee House. Hsu can be reached via encrypted message at andreahsu.08 on Signal. Andrew McClure Andrew McClure serves as the Director of the Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) at the U.S. Department of Energy, where he leads efforts to strengthen the security and resilience of the nation’s energy sector. As Director, he is responsible for hardening critical energy infrastructure, enhancing preparedness and response capabilities, and fostering partnerships across federal, state, local, and private-sector stakeholders to protect America’s energy systems against evolving cyber and physical threats. McClure is dedicated to continuing the bold and ambitious mission of President Donald J. Trump and U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright to safeguard the nation’s energy infrastructure and restore American energy dominance. Prior to returning to public service, McClure was a venture capitalist investing for over a decade in innovative technology companies critical to national security and economic competitiveness. At Forgepoint Capital he focused on cybersecurity and infrastructure software, and he partnered with entrepreneurs to build companies developing technologies that protect enterprises from evolving cyber threats. McClure also has over 30 years of cumulative board director experience.

pages.text: Andy Burnham urges caution on lifting Saturday 3pm TV blackout in UK - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 15:00 Saturday matches Published 16 November 2026 Andy Burnham has urged caution on lifting the Saturday 3pm TV blackout in the UK, saying the health of the football pyramid should come first. The rule was introduced in the 1960s to encourage fans to attend lower league games and prevents matches from being shown on UK television between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on Saturdays. The blackout, which is enforced by Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes and is imposed by the English and Scottish football associations, comes into effect when 50% of fixtures in the top two divisions are scheduled to kick off at 3pm. The Premier League is in the middle of a record £6.7bn domestic TV deal for Sky and TNT to show up to 270 live games a season. But there could be room for change with the 3pm rule in the upcoming broadcast cycle, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29. The prime minister said any decision to remove the ban would require careful thought about the consequences. "I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," Burnham said. pages.text: Anger as Cas overturns ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Since the end of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia have won the men's World Championship five times but have never claimed the women's title Published 30 October 2026 Ukraine's ice hockey federation has expressed "deep outrage" at Russia being allowed to compete in international events again. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban placed on Russia by the sport's global governing body, the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF). Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and earlier this year the IIHF ruled they would remain excluded. The Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) appealed that decision to Cas, which has upheld it following an in-person hearing at its headquarters in Lausanne, Switzerland. In a statement, the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said it "respected the authority and status of Cas". "At the same time, we express our deep outrage at this decision," it added. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Animas Forks | Colorado View Map In Full Screen Animas Forks is located on a system of roads known as the Alpine Loop. The loop is a 65-mile (105 kilometers) system of unpaved roads which connects the small mountain towns of Lake City, Ouray, and Silverton. Most of the land in the area is managed by either the U.S. Forest Service or the Bureau of Land Management. The Alpine Loop is visited by over 100,000 people each year. Animas Forks, at an elevation of 11,200 feet (3,400 meter), is more than two miles (3 kilometers) above sea level. The unimproved road from Silverton to Animas Forks is passable in summer by two-wheel drive vehicles. The road beyond Animas Forks over Engineer Pass to Lake City may require four-wheel drive. The town's first log cabin was built in 1873 and by 1876 the community had become a bustling mining community. At that time the town contained 30 cabins, a hotel, a general store, a saloon, and a post office. By 1883 450 people lived in Animas Forks and in 1882 a newspaper, the Animas Forks Pioneer, began publication and lasted until October 1886. Home » SBA leadership » Annie Spilman Download high-resolution image Annie Spilman Regional Administrator Annie Spilman serves as the South Central Regional Administrator for the U.S. Small Business Administration, overseeing operations and economic development across Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas. A seasoned legislative strategist with over 25 years of public policy experience, Ms. Spilman previously founded MainStreet Relations and served as the Texas state director for the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB). She began her career in the Texas House of Representatives in 2000 and is widely recognized for building bipartisan coalitions and advocating for Main Street job creators across state media. A sixth-generation Texan and graduate of Texas State University, Ms. Spilman is committed to expanding access to capital and eliminating barriers for entrepreneurs throughout the South Central Region.

Guided by strong leadership from the Ministry of Health and supported by WHO and partners—including the Pandemic Fund—Bhutan advanced critical capacities across laboratories, surveillance, One Health, pandemic preparedness, and point-of-entry (PoE) readiness. Bhutan made significant progress in strengthening laboratory systems and diagnostic readiness, enhancing early detection and response capacities for priority diseases. With support from the Pandemic Fund through WHO, the Royal Centre for Disease Control (RCDC) received Nu. 19.3 million (USD 220,216) worth of advanced laboratory equipment, including ELISA systems, biosafety cabinets, PCR kits, and essential biosafety supplies. These investments substantially improved the country’s capacity to detect respiratory pathogens, zoonotic diseases, and emerging public health threats with greater speed, accuracy, and safety. pages.text: Annual Survey of Public Employment & Payroll Summary Report: 2025 Annual Survey of Public Employment & Payroll Summary Report: 2025 Skip Navigation Within Census Bureau Library Annual Survey of Public Employment & Payroll Summary Report: 2025 April 16, 2026 Written by: ROSS JACOBSON, JAMI SEGAL, JENNIFER WENNING, and SEAN WILBURN Report Number: G25-ASPEP Introduction Download Annual Survey of Public Employment & Payroll Summary Report: 2025 [PDF - <1.0 MB] In March 2025, state and local governments employed 20.3 million people, an increase of 1.4 percent from the 2024 figure of 20.0 million. Nationally, local government workers comprised the majority of the state and local government workforce with 14.7 million employees (72.2 percent). In comparison, state governments employed 5.7 million workers (27.8 percent). Of the total 20.3 million employed, 15.8 million were classified as full-time and 4.5 million as part-time. Full-time employment by state governments increased by 2.7 percent to 4.1 million, while full-time employment by local governments increased 1.2 percent to 11.7 million. The number of part-time state government employees increased 0.8 percent to 1.5 million. Part-time local government employees increased 0.8 percent to 3.0 million. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Ant Hills WSA | Colorado View Map In Full Screen The remote Ant Hills Wilderness Study Area (WSA) consists of hills and valleys on the southern slopes of Douglas Mountain, which trend southward into Dinosaur National Monument and the Yampa River. The Ant Hills consist of several hills rising 400 to 500 feet above the draws in the southeastern part of the WSA. The area is an extension of the landforms and upper end of drainages found in Dinosaur National Monument. There are no developed recreation sites in the Douglas Mountain area, but the area offers opportunities for visitors to enjoy deer and elk hunting, camping, sightseeing, hiking, backpacking and horseback riding. Motorized and mechanized vehicle travel is limited to existing roads and trails within these WSAs. Vegetation consists mainly of ponderosa pine, pinyon-juniper woodlands, sagebrush, and native grass communities. Fauna includes mule deer, elk, raptors and other birds, and various small mammals and reptiles. pages.text: Antique Road Show Skip to main content The fabled road (a c. 1955 postcard) stretched 2,448 miles. National Museum of American History, Transportation Collection, Smithsonian Institution Back when the Model A Ford was America's ticket to ride, it must have seemed that half the nation was heading west on Route 66. In fact, the late songwriter Bobby Troup penned "Get Your Kicks on Route 66" during his own trip west on that legendary highway just after World War II, not only launching a songwriting career but also placing the road in the mythos of America. Those who took to the highway in the 1930s to escape drought in the Midwest and cross the desert to California might have been more inclined, if you'll allow me a complete anachronism, to hum a few bars of the hard-rock classic "Highway to Hell." What it was, more accurately, was a highway from hell, with the hope of a paradise at the western end of a paved rainbow. In today's age of major four- and six-lane thoroughfares to and from just about everywhere, it's not easy to conceive just how powerfully one stretch of two-lane highway could grip America's collective imagination. This country has historically looked west for a better tomorrow—Daniel Boone and his fellow woodsmen headed for the setting sun as soon as they could see three or four cabins from their homesteads. pages.text: API for the National Archives Catalog | National Archives Top Skip to main content API for the National Archives Catalog About the Catalog API On This Page Terms of Use Gaining Access Rate Limits Use Right to Limit Changes Technical Support Disclaimer Related Pages National Archives Catalog API Getting Started with the Catalog API Catalog API GitHub Catalog API Scripts on GitHub Catalog API Swagger Contact the Catalog API Team Catalog_API@nara.gov The National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) offers some of its public data for all of the records in the Catalog in machine readable format via the Catalog Application Programming Interface (API). The open-source Catalog API supports public access to NARA records, facilitates research, and spurs innovation. Application developers can incorporate archival data and metadata into their applications, websites, or datasets. The API provides access to all available archival descriptions, authority records, metadata about digital objects (i.e. images, videos, etc.), extracted text (such as optical character recognition or OCR text), and public contributions (tags, transcriptions, and comments). The API allows researchers and developers to retrieve metadata in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format for any given record or search results set. This method offers added flexibility for advanced search and refinement because the API can search and retrieve using keywords for any field in the system, search within ranges, apply sorts, specify only particular fields to return, or any combination of these options. pages.text: Archaeologists found 37 people buried in one giant 'death jar' | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Archaeologists found 37 people buried in one giant 'death jar' A newly excavated megalithic container holding skeletal remains in Laos may help finally solve the mystery of the so-called "Plain of Jars." The discovery of bones and other artifacts inside a giant stone jar on the Xieng Khouang Plateau of Laos suggests the megalithic vessel may have served as a communal burial site for centuries. Daniel Baker By Meghie Rodrigues Published July 31, 2026 Located in northern Laos, the Xieng Khouang Plateau is home to one of the world's most puzzling archaeological sites: the Plain of Jars. The name comes from the hundreds of stone “jars” scattered around the area. For nearly a century, archaeologists have pondered their purpose, suspecting they were funerary urns, as some had been found with burnt bones and ashes. Now a team of researchers exploring the site has found a hefty, megalithic stone jar containing the remains of at least 37 people—from a toddler to adults—that dates to more than a thousand years ago. “We were very excited because it was the first time we found non-burnt bones inside a jar,” says Nicholas Skopal , an archaeologist at James Cook University in Australia and lead author of the study, which was published in spring in A ntiquity . The skeletal remains inside the jars were not tossed in randomly, Skopal says, as large bones and skulls were set near the outer edges. pages.text: Ardipithecus: We Meet At Last | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Ardipithecus: We Meet At Last By Carl Zimmer Published October 1, 2009 • 10 min read Meet Ardipithecus . This introduction has been a long time coming. Some 4.4 million years ago, a hominid now known as Ardipithecus ramidus lived in what were then forests in Ethiopia. Fifteen years ago, Tim White of Berkeley and a team of Ethiopian and American scientists published the first account of Ardipithecus , which they had just discovered. But it was just a preliminary report, and White promised more details later, once he and his colleagues had carefully prepared and analyzed all the fossils they had unearthed. “Later,” it turned out, meant 15 years. I’ve mentioned before how unfashionable this slow-cooked style of science can be. But sometimes, it’s the only way to do things right. Getting clues about HIV by observing sick chimpanzees in the wild takes years. And so does reconstructing a fossil–particularly one as delicate as Ardipithecus happened to be. Today, the journal Science has handed many of its pages over to White and his colleagues, who have filled them with lots of details about Ardipithecus , plus a couple excellent articles by writer Ann Gibbons. Ardipithecus has gone from being an enigmatic collection of bones to a new touchstone for our early hominid ancestors. Scientists are turning to a surprising ally in the battle against drug-resistant bacteria: A special type of virus found in our most polluted places. By Jess Craig Published December 16, 2022 • 13 min read Nairobi, KENYA — Early one morning in October, Lillian Musila, Martin Georges, and Moses Gachoya packed lab coats, medical gloves, and plastic coolers into a white Toyota 4X4, departed the manicured grounds of the Kenya Medical Research Institute campus, and set off for the outskirts of town. Their destinations are the dirtiest, germ-teeming places that come to mind: sewage treatment plants, polluted rivers, the wastewater that runs between the densely packed, tin-roofed shops and homes in Kibera, one of Africa’s largest slums.
